questions.q: In the same record, Eritrea's forest cover fell from $$30\%$$ in 1912 to $$5\%$$ in 1960. Calculate the average annual decrease in forest cover over 1912 to 1960, in percentage points per year.
questions.answer: The average annual decrease was approximately $$0.52\text{ percentage points per year}$$.
why: **List the values and the time span.** 1912 cover = $$30\%$$; 1960 cover = $$5\%$$; time elapsed = $$1960 - 1912 = 48\text{ years}$$.
**Compute the total decline.** Decline = $$30\% - 5\% = 25\text{ percentage points}$$.
**Divide by the number of years.** Average annual decrease = $$\dfrac{25}{48} = 0.5208\ldots \approx 0.52\text{ percentage points per year}$$.

questions.q: A forest block of $$10\text{ hectares}$$ in the Semenawi-Bahri highlands is surveyed and found to have a tree canopy covering $$15\,000\text{ m}^2$$. Using the unit's classification by canopy density, how should this forest be classified?

options.A: As an open forest, because its canopy coverage is at least $$10\%$$ with a discontinuous canopy.
options.B: As a closed forest, because its canopy coverage exceeds $$20\%$$.
options.C: As a primary forest, because the canopy is undisturbed by human activity.
options.D: As an uneven-aged forest, because canopy cover varies from place to place.

why: **Convert the forest area to square metres.** $$1\text{ hectare} = 10\,000\text{ m}^2$$, so the block covers $$10 \times 10\,000 = 100\,000\text{ m}^2$$.
**Find the percentage canopy coverage.** Canopy coverage $$= \dfrac{15\,000\text{ m}^2}{100\,000\text{ m}^2} \times 100\% = 15\%$$.

**Apply the canopy-density definitions.** A closed forest has canopy coverage greater than $$20\%$$; an open forest has discontinuous canopy coverage of at least $$10\%$$ with a continuous grass layer underneath. Since $$15\%$$ is below $$20\%$$ but above $$10\%$$, the block is an open forest.

**Check the distractors one by one.** B is wrong because $$15\%$$ does not exceed $$20\%$$. C is wrong because primary forest is a classification by level of human interference, not by canopy density. D is wrong because even-aged or uneven-aged is a classification by age, and canopy variation is not the stated criterion. Only A states a criterion and conclusion consistent with the unit, so it is the unique correct option.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: A 40-hectare dry montane forest near Nakfa has a tree canopy covering $$96\,000\text{ m}^2$$. Classify this forest by canopy density using the unit's definitions.

why: **Convert hectares to square metres.** $$40\text{ hectares} = 40 \times 10\,000 = 400\,000\text{ m}^2$$.
**Calculate the canopy percentage.** Coverage $$= \dfrac{96\,000}{400\,000} \times 100\% = 24\%$$.
**Compare with the threshold.** A closed forest has canopy coverage greater than $$20\%$$. Since $$24\% > 20\%$$, the forest is closed.

questions.q: According to the unit, a forest whose canopy coverage is greater than $$20\%$$ is classified as a ______ forest, while a forest with discontinuous canopy coverage of at least $$10\%$$ and a continuous grass layer underneath is classified as an ______ forest.
questions.answer: A closed forest (greater than $$20\%$$ canopy coverage) and an open forest (discontinuous canopy of at least $$10\%$$ with a continuous grass layer underneath).
why: **Recall the canopy-density classes.** The unit classifies forests by canopy density into closed forest and open forest, using canopy coverage as the distinguishing measure.

**Match each definition to its term.** Greater than $$20\%$$ canopy coverage defines a closed forest; discontinuous canopy coverage of at least $$10\%$$ with a continuous grass layer underneath defines an open forest.

questions.q: A restoration team is given a fixed supply of $$5\,000$$ tree seedlings for a dry site on the Buri Peninsula. The unit states that the standard spacing of $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ gives a density of $$2\,500\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$, and that in drier areas the spacing is increased to $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ to reduce competition for water. (a) Calculate the number of seedlings per hectare at the wider $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ spacing. (b) Determine how many hectares the $$5\,000$$ seedlings can plant at this dry-site spacing, and state how much more area this covers than the same $$5\,000$$ seedlings would cover at the standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing.
questions.answer: (a) $$1\,111\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$ (exactly $$\frac{10\,000}{9}$$) at $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ spacing. (b) The $$5\,000$$ seedlings can plant $$4.5\text{ hectares}$$ at the dry-site spacing, which is $$2.5\text{ hectares}$$ more than the $$2\text{ hectares}$$ they would plant at the standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing.
why: **Establish the area occupied by one seedling.** At $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ spacing each seedling occupies a square of side $$3\text{ m}$$, so each seedling occupies $$3 \times 3 = 9\text{ m}^2$$.
**Convert one hectare to square metres.** $$1\text{ hectare} = 10\,000\text{ m}^2$$, the unit conversion needed to express the density per hectare.

**Calculate the density at $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$.** (a) Density $$= \dfrac{10\,000\text{ m}^2\text{ per hectare}}{9\text{ m}^2\text{ per seedling}} = 1\,111.1\ldots \approx 1\,111\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$.

**Cross-check the density with the standard spacing.** For comparison, the unit's standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing gives $$\dfrac{10\,000}{4} = 2\,500\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$, which matches the unit value and confirms the method. Widening the spacing from $$2\text{ m}$$ to $$3\text{ m}$$ therefore more than halves the number of seedlings needed per hectare.

**Find the area plantable at the dry-site spacing.** (b) Area $$= \dfrac{\text{number of seedlings}}{\text{density}} = \dfrac{5\,000\text{ seedlings}}{1\,111.1\text{ seedlings per hectare}} = 4.5\text{ hectares}$$. Equivalently, $$5\,000 \times 9\text{ m}^2 = 45\,000\text{ m}^2 = 4.5\text{ hectares}$$.
**Find the area the same supply would cover at standard spacing.** At $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$, area $$= \dfrac{5\,000}{2\,500} = 2\text{ hectares}$$.

**Compare the two areas and conclude.** The extra area covered $$= 4.5 - 2 = 2.5\text{ hectares}$$. So $$5\,000$$ seedlings plant $$4.5$$ hectares at the dry-site spacing of $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$, which is $$2.5$$ hectares more than the same supply would plant at the standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing. This is why the unit recommends wider spacing in drier areas: each seedling has more soil water available and competition for water is reduced.

questions.q: A nursery allocates $$9\,000$$ seedlings to a dry lowland enclosure site along the Anseba where foresters decide to use the wider $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ spacing ($$1\,111\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$) instead of the standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ ($$2\,500\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$). (a) How many hectares can be planted at $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$? (b) How many hectares would the same $$9\,000$$ seedlings have covered at $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$, and what is the difference?
questions.answer: (a) $$8.1\text{ hectares}$$ at $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$. (b) $$3.6\text{ hectares}$$ at $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$, a difference of $$4.5\text{ hectares}$$.
why: **Use the dry-site density.** At $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ each seedling occupies $$9\text{ m}^2$$, giving $$\dfrac{10\,000}{9} \approx 1\,111\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$.
**Calculate the area at the wider spacing.** (a) Area $$= \dfrac{9\,000}{1\,111.1} = 8.1\text{ hectares}$$; equivalently $$9\,000 \times 9 = 81\,000\text{ m}^2 = 8.1\text{ hectares}$$.
**Calculate the area at the standard spacing.** (b) Area $$= \dfrac{9\,000}{2\,500} = 3.6\text{ hectares}$$.
**Compare and conclude.** Difference $$= 8.1 - 3.6 = 4.5\text{ hectares}$$, so the wider spacing allows the same nursery supply to cover $$4.5$$ hectares more land.

questions.q: In a Parkland Agroforestry system, multipurpose trees such as Balanites aegyptiaca and Faidherbia albida are kept at widely spaced intervals of $$10\text{ to }20\text{ trees per hectare}$$ among annual crops. questions.answer: (a) $$1\,000\text{ m}^2$$ of land per tree at $$10\text{ trees per hectare}$$. (b) Wide spacing lets the trees provide livestock feed, fuel wood and shade without blocking too much sunlight from the crops growing below.

cards.title: 3.1.1 What soil and water conservation means
body: **Soil and water conservation (SWC)** = all the human activities that **keep soil on the land** and **protect and maintain the water supply**: practical farming measures that stop land damage and water waste.

Soil and water go together: a terrace that stops soil washing away also holds the rain so it soaks in. Some measures are mainly for water (ponds, dams), others mainly for soil (bunds, grass strips), but most do both.

**Eritrean examples you can see:** stone bunds and terraces on the hillsides around Asmara and Mendefera, micro-basins with seedlings planted by students in the summer campaign, check dams in gullies, enclosures on steep slopes, ponds and small dams such as **Toker** near Asmara.

cards.title: 3.1.2 Why SWC matters so much in Eritrea
body: Eritrea lies in the **Sudano-Sahelian** belt: rain is **low, erratic** and **badly distributed**; much of the country is too dry for rain-fed farming. Farming has gone on for thousands of years, and local SWC methods (terraces, bunds) are old.
**The size of the problem:**
- On poorly conserved land, soil is lost **20–40 times faster** than it forms.

- Measured water erosion in the **highlands**: **3.4 to 84.5 t/ha a year**, mean **42 t/ha** (about 3–4 mm of topsoil a year, some 20 times the rate of formation). The highlands have the **greatest livestock density** and the worst degradation.
- Erosion can cut yields by **30–90 %** on shallow soils; some Eritrean land has lost **50 %** of its productivity.
- Nutrient depletion: about **22 kg N, 3 kg P and 15 kg K per hectare per year**.
- Average cereal yield in Eritrea is only **0.74 t/ha**, while good soil management elsewhere has raised it from 1 to 5–6 t/ha.

**Benefits of SWC:** more organic matter, so more water held and more infiltration, less runoff; **less silt in dams** (they last longer); ponds and dams allow **irrigation** and high-value crops; restored land can be farmed again; **higher productivity**.

cards.title: How fast Eritrea loses soil
body: The highlands lose the most: steep slopes, intense storms, many animals and little cover.

cards.title: Turning t/ha into millimetres of soil
cards.problem: Soil loss is 42 t/ha per year and topsoil weighs about 1.3 t per m³. How many mm of soil is lost each year?

steps.text: 1 ha = 10 000 m², so 42 t/ha = 42 000 kg ÷ 10 000 m² = 4.2 kg per m².
Volume = 4.2 kg ÷ 1 300 kg/m³ ≈ 0.0032 m³ per m².
Depth = 0.0032 m ≈ 3.2 mm a year.

cards.answer: About 3 mm a year (the textbook rounds to 4 mm); 1 cm of topsoil gone in about 3 years.

cards.problem: What percentage of topsoil and organic matter is primarily lost during sheet erosion?

steps.text: **Reasoning**
Sheet erosion involves the removal of a thin, uniform layer of topsoil over a wide area.
Because organic matter and key nutrients are concentrated in the topsoil (the uppermost layer), sheet erosion selectively strips away this most fertile portion of the soil.
**Conclusion**
Therefore, the correct answer is **The most fertile upper layer.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the primary agent responsible for the physical soil degradation known as wind deflation in dry plains?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Deflation is the process by which wind lifts and removes loose, fine-grained, dry particles from the soil surface. This occurs primarily in arid and semi-arid climates where wind velocities are high and vegetation cover is scanty.

**Conclusion**
Therefore, the primary agent is **High-velocity wind**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: According to standard definitions, soil salinization in irrigated fields is primarily caused by which of the following?

options.A: The loss of nitrogenous organic matter.
options.B: The accumulation of excess soluble salts in the root zone.
options.C: The physical compaction of topsoil by machinery.
options.D: The direct impact of high-velocity raindrops.
options.E: An excessive rate of cover crop nitrogen fixation.

cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Salinization is the accumulation of water-soluble salts in the soil profile, particularly in the root zone of crops. It commonly becomes a problem in arid areas under irrigation when poor-quality, saline water is applied without adequate drainage.

**Conclusion**
Thus, salinization is **the accumulation of excess soluble salts in the root zone**.

cards.title: 3.2.1 Land degradation and its components
body: **Land degradation** = a fall in the present or future ability of land to produce goods and services. It is both a **process** (gradual weakening of the land) and a **result**: smaller farms per household, falling crop and livestock yields, lost vegetation, fuelwood shortage, lost topsoil.
**Immediate causes:** **over-cultivation, overgrazing and deforestation**, made worse by drought.
**Four components:** soil degradation, vegetation degradation, biodiversity degradation and water degradation (see figure).
**Soil degradation** has three kinds:

- **Physical**: **erosion** (the main one; water erosion everywhere, wind erosion on the coast and in the north-western lowlands), loss of structure because residues are burnt or fed to animals, **compaction** and hard pans, crusting.

- **Chemical**: loss of **nutrients and organic matter** (harvests and residues removed and not replaced), nutrients **fixed** in strongly alkaline soils, **salinisation** (salt build-up, especially under irrigation with poor water, e.g. on the coast), acidification, sodication, laterisation.
- **Biological**: organic matter down to **under 1 %** in many Eritrean soils; fewer earthworms, termites and microbes that build structure, fix nitrogen and decompose residues.

cards.title: 3.2.2 Causes of land degradation
body: Causes are **natural** and **human**, and they combine with social, economic and political factors.

**Population:** one view blames population pressure for deforestation, overgrazing and farming of marginal land. But **it is what people do with the land that matters**: healthy, motivated farmers with secure rights can **reverse** degradation, and densely settled areas are often centres of land-care innovation (the terraced hills of the Eritrean highlands are an example). Poverty, illiteracy and insecure land tenure make degradation worse.

cards.title: 3.2.3 Soil erosion
body: **Erosion** = soil and rock particles **detached and carried away** by water, wind, ice, gravity (creep) or living things, and deposited elsewhere. It is natural, but people speed it up greatly by clearing vegetation and ploughing. **Weathering** is different: it breaks rock down **in place**.
**What controls the rate:**
- **Climate**: amount and **intensity** of rain, wind, storms.
- **Geology / soil**: rock and soil type, **porosity and permeability**, **slope**. Sandy and silty soils and steep slopes erode easily; clay resists more.
- **Biology**: **ground cover** (the factor people change most) and land use. In a forest, litter and roots protect the soil; once trees are cut, infiltration falls and erosion rises.
Erosion removes the fertile topsoil, exposes roots and fills dams and reservoirs with silt.

cards.title: Note on gully depth
body: The textbook says gullies may be "75 to 150 metres" deep. Most gullies are **from about 0.5 m to a few tens of metres** deep; channels 100 m deep are canyons. Also, ice and snow-melt erosion do not occur in Eritrea.

cards.title: Soil losses and their cost in Eritrea
body: - Net loss from **croplands**: about **12 t/ha a year**, because **fallowing and rotation** are used less and less, and farms get smaller as population grows.
- Estimated loss: **highlands 50–100 t/ha**, **moist lowlands 47**, **eastern escarpment 37**, **dry lowlands 6 t/ha** a year.
- Consequences: less organic matter, so less water stored and less infiltration; crops suffer more in drought; poor regrowth of vegetation; fertility decline.
- **Dung burned as fuel** in the highlands: about **273 000 t a year**. With 1.4 % N and 1.3 % P, that is about **3 800 t of nitrogen and 3 500 t of phosphorus** lost every year.

cards.problem: Burnt dung loses 3 800 t of nitrogen a year. Urea contains 46 % N. How much urea would replace it?

steps.text: Urea needed = N ÷ 0.46.

cards.answer: About 8 300 t of urea every year, just for the nitrogen.

cards.title: Explaining the chain of land degradation
cards.problem: Explain how overgrazing on a hillside can lead to land degradation and suggest two remedies.

steps.text: Too many animals eat the grass faster than it regrows, leaving bare soil.
Hooves compact and loosen the soil; bare soil is exposed to raindrop splash and runoff.
Topsoil and nutrients are washed away → rills and gullies form → lower productivity (land degradation).
Remedies: reduce stocking rates / rotational grazing, and area closures with tree and grass planting, plus terraces or bunds to slow runoff.

cards.answer: Overgrazing removes plant cover → erosion of topsoil → loss of productivity. Remedies: controlled grazing and area closure/reforestation with soil-conservation structures.

options.A: the building of terraces on slopes

**Step 2:** Continued degradation permanently reduces biological potential and living conditions.

**Tip:** In essay answers separate natural and human causes.

cards.title: 3.3 SWC measures: biological and physical
body: SWC measures are chosen for the **site** and its problem. Two broad groups, best used **together**:
- **Biological (vegetative / agronomic)**: plants and farming practices: enclosures, afforestation, grass strips, cover crops, mulch, rotation, agroforestry.
- **Physical (mechanical / structural)**: earth and stone works: terraces, stone bunds, check dams, diversion ditches, waterways, gabions.
A stone bund protects a field at once; grass planted on it makes it stronger every year.

cards.title: Biological measures
body: Enclosures · afforestation · grass strips · cover crops · mulch · crop rotation and intercropping · manure · agroforestry · riverbank planting. They **cover the soil** and **add organic matter**.

cards.title: Physical measures
body: Hillside, bench and broad- or narrow-based terraces · stone and soil bunds · micro-basins · check dams · cut-off/diversion ditches · waterways · gabions · land levelling. They **shorten the slope** and **slow the water**.

cards.title: 3.3.1 Surveying for SWC
body: Before building structures you must measure distances, heights and slopes and mark **contours**.
- **Horizontal interval (HI)**: horizontal distance between two points (used on maps).
- **Vertical interval (VI)**: difference in height between them.
- **Slope** can be given as an **angle** (degrees), a **percentage** (VI ÷ HI × 100), a **ratio** 1 : n (vertical always 1) or **metres per metre** (e.g. 0.4 % = 0.004 m/m for a canal).
- Slope classes: **0–8 %** level to gently undulating, **8–30 %** rolling to hilly, **over 30 %** steep to mountainous.
- **Contour**: a line joining points of the **same height**. **Levelling**: measuring height differences; **profile levelling** at fixed distances along a line.

**Instruments:** chain and tape (a surveyor's chain is **20 m or 30 m** long), **line level**, **clinometer** (hand-held, reads % slope and degrees), **flexible-tube (water) level**, **magnetic compass** (bearings: N 0°, E 90°, S 180°, W 270°), **telescopic level** (most accurate, most expensive).

cards.title: Expressing one slope four ways
cards.problem: Two pegs are 40 m apart horizontally, and one is 6 m higher. Give the slope as a percentage, a ratio, in m/m and as an angle, and classify it.

steps.text: Percentage = VI ÷ HI × 100 = 6 ÷ 40 × 100 = 15 %.
Angle: tan θ = 0.15, so θ ≈ 8.5°.
15 % lies in 8–30 %: rolling to hilly.

cards.answer: 15 %, 1 : 6.7, 0.15 m/m, about 8.5°; rolling to hilly land.

cards.title: Watch out: per cent is not degrees
body: A 100 % slope is **45°** (VI = HI), not vertical. Activity 3.5 (HI 60 m, VI 120 m) gives **200 %**, about **63°**: a cliff, not farmland, but the formula is the same.

cards.title: Line level
body: Two identical 1.5 m sticks, 10 m apart, joined by a cotton string tied at the 0 mark; a small spirit level hangs in the middle. Move the second stick up or down the slope until the bubble is centred: both pegs are then on the same contour.

cards.title: Water-tube level
body: Water finds its own level: when the two poles stand at the same height, the water in both ends is at the same mark.

cards.title: Textbook check: chain length and map scale
body: - The textbook says the metric chain is "30 **cm**" long. It is **20 m or 30 m**.
- It says on a 1 : 1 000 map "1 cm = 1 000 **m**". Wrong: 1 cm on the map = 1 000 **cm** = **10 m** on the ground, so 3 cm = **30 m**, not 3 000 m.
- "Much more expressive" for the telescopic level should read "much more **expensive**".

cards.title: Map scale and area
cards.problem: On a 1 : 2 000 plan, a rectangular field measures 4 cm by 2.5 cm. Find its real size and area in hectares.

steps.text: 1 cm on the plan = 2 000 cm = 20 m.

cards.title: Large scale vs small scale
body: **Large-scale** map (1 : 1 000) = **small area, much detail** (a farm plan). **Small-scale** map (1 : 100 000) = **large area, little detail** (a zoba map). Big fraction = large scale.

cards.title: 3.3.2 Physical SWC measures
body: Earthworks that **cut the slope into short sections**, so runoff is caught and slowed before it gains speed, soaks into the soil and recharges groundwater.
- **Hillside terraces**: ditches or ridges on the contour for runoff control on uncultivated slopes.
- **Bench terraces**: level steps, like a staircase, for crops on steep land.
- **Broad-based** (gentle slopes, can be cropped over) and **narrow-based** terraces.
- **Stone bunds**: stone walls on the contour; soil collects behind them and the field slowly becomes terraced. Very common on Eritrean farms.
- **Micro-basins**: small half-moon basins round each seedling, staggered so runoff missed by one is caught by the next.
- **Check dams**: walls of stone (or gabions, brushwood) across a gully; silt fills behind them and the gully heals. Key them into the banks and leave a lower spillway in the centre.
- **Diversion (cut-off) ditches** lead runoff safely away from fields into **waterways**; **land levelling** for irrigation.

cards.title: Spacing stone bunds
cards.problem: Bunds are placed so that the height difference between them (VI) is 1 m. On a 10 % slope, how far apart (HI) should they be? How many bunds fit on a 200 m long slope?

steps.text: % slope = VI ÷ HI × 100, so HI = VI × 100 ÷ % slope.
200 ÷ 10 = 20 spaces, so about 20 bunds.

cards.answer: Every 10 m; about 20 bunds. (On a 20 % slope they would be 5 m apart: steeper land needs closer structures.)

cards.title: 3.3.3 Biological SWC measures
body: Plants protect the soil with **cover** (no splash), **roots** (hold soil) and **organic matter** (more infiltration). Use them:
- on **uncultivated hillsides**: **enclosures** and **afforestation**;
- on **cropland**: **agronomic** measures and **agroforestry** (parkland trees, windbreaks, grass and shrubs planted on bunds);
- on **riverbanks**: protect riverine vegetation and plant suitable species with **gabions**.

cards.title: 3.3.4 Agronomic practices and good land husbandry
body: **Agronomic practices** = ways of managing crops that also conserve soil and water: **manure and fertiliser** (more growth = more cover), **cover crops**, **crop rotation and intercropping**, **crop-residue and organic-matter management**, **mulching**, appropriate **tillage**, **trash lines** and **contour strip-cropping**.
- **Soil management** = all tillage, cropping, fertiliser and lime treatments applied to a soil.
- **Water management** = conserving and using rain, flood and soil water with minimum waste.
- **Land husbandry** = caring for, managing and improving land, like animal or crop husbandry.

- **Conservation agriculture** = farming that keeps soil covered and disturbed as little as possible (rotation, cover crops, minimum or zero tillage, stubble mulch) to keep moisture all season; it suits Eritrea's dry areas.
Major soil problems to manage: acidity, salinity, alkalinity, compaction, erosion, and swelling–shrinking clays.

cards.title: 3.4 Water harvesting
body: Earth has plenty of water, but **fresh water** is scarce. **Water harvesting** = collecting and storing rain and runoff for people, animals and crops; it can turn rain-fed farming into irrigated farming.

Options: **roof** harvesting, ponds and small dams on seasonal rivers, large dams on major rivers (without harming local communities), **diversion** of seasonal floods (**spate**), **fog harvesting** on the misty eastern escarpment, **desalination** of sea and brackish water, and **artificial groundwater recharge**. Households, community organisations, NGOs and government all have to invest.

cards.title: 3.4.1 Dams
body: A **dam** blocks a river to store water in a **reservoir** for **drinking, livestock, irrigation, hydro-power and flood control**. Earth dams have an earth embankment with an **impervious clay core** to stop seepage, and a **spillway** to pass floods safely. Example: **Toker dam** near Asmara; many micro-dams across the highlands.
**Disadvantages:** costly; silt fills the reservoir if the catchment is bare; water lost by evaporation; land flooded; still water can breed mosquitoes and snails (malaria, bilharzia).

cards.title: 3.4.2 Ponds
body: A **pond** is made by digging a pit or by building a short embankment across a watercourse. In Eritrea ponds are small, about **500–5 000 m³**, and used for short periods, mostly in arid areas. On flat land dig; on a slope use the dug soil to build an embankment and store more.
Uses: **livestock**, **household water**, **small-scale irrigation** of vegetables. Fence them and keep animals out to keep the water clean.

cards.title: How long will a pond last?
cards.problem: A 3 000 m³ pond supplies 200 cattle (40 L each a day) and loses 5 mm of depth a day by evaporation over a surface of 1 500 m². About how many days will it last?

steps.text: Cattle use 200 × 40 = 8 000 L = 8 m³ a day.
Evaporation = 1 500 m² × 0.005 m = 7.5 m³ a day.
Total ≈ 15.5 m³ a day.

cards.answer: About 190 days (around 6 months); evaporation uses almost half the water.

cards.title: 3.4.3 River diversion
body: A **diversion structure** across a river sends a controlled amount of water into a **canal**. Examples: the diversion works at **Sheeb** (Northern Red Sea) and the canals around **Megolo** (Gash-Barka). Diversion is the heart of **spate irrigation**.

cards.title: 3.4.4 Wells
body: Wells are a major source of water for irrigation and homes. **Open (hand-dug) wells** are dug in **riverbeds, valleys and flat land** (never on hilltops), and can be lined with stone and cement. **Drilled (tube) wells** with a pump are used mostly for homes and livestock.

A **sub-surface dam** is a wall of clay or masonry built down to the rock across a sandy riverbed; it holds water in the sand where it does not evaporate. Put the **well on the upstream side, close to the dam**.

cards.title: Textbook check: "no perennial rivers"
body: The textbook says Eritrea has "no perennial rivers". The **Setit (Tekeze)** on the south-western border flows all year; most other rivers (Gash, Barka, Anseba, Mereb) are **seasonal**. So: Eritrea has **very few** perennial rivers.

cards.title: 3.4.5 Roof and rock-outcrop harvesting
body: **Concrete** and **corrugated-iron** roofs are excellent catchments: gutters lead the rain into a **concrete cistern** for drinking and small vegetable gardens. Bare **rock outcrops** can be used the same way, with low walls leading the runoff into a tank.
**Rule of thumb:** water collected (m³) ≈ roof area (m²) × rainfall (m) × 0.8 (some water is lost by splashing and evaporation).

cards.title: Sizing a cistern
cards.problem: A school roof is 12 m × 8 m. Asmara gets about 500 mm of rain a year. How much water can be collected, and how many 200 L drums would it fill?

steps.text: Area = 12 × 8 = 96 m².
Rain = 500 mm = 0.5 m.

cards.answer: About 38 m³ (38 400 L) a year, enough for about 190 drums.

cards.title: 3.5 Irrigation and drainage: the big picture
body: Water management on a farm means getting **enough water to the roots** (irrigation) and **taking away excess water and salt** (drainage). Both are needed: irrigation without drainage ends in waterlogging and salty soil.

cards.title: 3.5.1 Irrigation
body: **Irrigation** = artificial application of water to the soil, carried from the source to the crop in open canals or pipes. Farming that depends only on rain is **rain-fed**. Irrigation is very old: evidence from Mesopotamia, Egypt and Iran goes back to the **6th millennium BCE**.
Other uses: protecting crops from frost, controlling weeds, preventing soil consolidation.

cards.title: 3.5.2 Why irrigation matters
body: - In arid and semi-arid areas it **extends cultivation**, **raises yields** and **insures against unreliable rain**; in humid areas **supplementary irrigation** covers dry spells at critical stages.
- Water comes from **surface water** (rivers, dams) or **groundwater** (wells); groundwater also lowers a high water table.
- Eritrea's potential irrigable area is **107 000–567 000 ha** (the upper figure counts all land that is topographically suitable).
- Irrigation allows **multiple cropping**, a more varied diet (vegetables, fruit), better nutrition and health, income, rural jobs, and **cheaper food** for the urban poor.
- **Risks:** waterlogging, salinity, water-borne diseases, high costs and conflicts over water: irrigation is not always beneficial unless well managed.

cards.title: 3.5.3 Methods of irrigation
body: The aim is to wet the whole field **evenly**, neither too much nor too little.
**Surface (traditional) irrigation**: water flows over the land by **gravity**. Cheap to build, but **labour-costly to run** and **inefficient** (40–50 %).
- **Furrow**: water runs in furrows between ridges; widespread in Eritrea (e.g. banana farms near **Tesseney**).
- **Basin**: level plots surrounded by earth bunds are flooded.
- **Border strip**: long strips between low ridges.
- **Spate**: diverts floods from highland rains into bunded fields; widely used in the **eastern lowlands** (Sheeb, Wadi Laba) and introduced in the western lowlands.
**Modern (pressurised / localised)**: expensive to install, cheap to run, efficient.
- **Sprinkler**: spray from pipes or rotating heads; about **75 %** reaches the crop; irrigate at **night** to cut evaporation.

- **Drip (trickle)**: drops at each plant's roots; the most efficient (up to about 90 %); fertiliser can be added (**fertigation**); often combined with plastic mulch; high cost for subsistence farmers.
- **Centre pivot**: a long sprinkler pipe on wheeled towers turning round a central point; on flat lowlands such as **Gerset** and **Fanko**.
- **Sub-irrigation**: raising the water table so roots are wetted from below; used in greenhouses with nutrient solution recycled.

cards.title: Water saved by changing method
cards.problem: A tomato plot needs 3 000 m³ of water to reach the roots in a season. How much water must be supplied with furrow (45 % efficient) and with drip (90 %)?

steps.text: Water supplied = water needed ÷ efficiency.
Saving ≈ 3 340 m³, half the water.

cards.answer: Furrow ≈ 6 670 m³, drip ≈ 3 330 m³: drip halves the water bill.

cards.title: 3.5.4 Drainage
body: **Drainage** = removing **excess water** from the surface and the upper subsoil. Waterlogged soil has **no air**: roots suffocate, toxic substances build up, microbes stop working, the soil is hard to cultivate and is damaged by ploughing.
**Causes of poor drainage:** heavy rain; **clay** soils that let water through slowly; permeable sand or gravel lying over an **impermeable clay layer**; **hard pans** in the subsoil.

cards.title: 3.5.5 Why drainage matters, even in dry areas
body: - Even a **week** of waterlogging can kill fruit trees.

- In dry areas, **irrigation water always carries salts**. Evaporation and transpiration remove the water and leave the salt, which can reach toxic levels (**salinisation**). Fields need occasional **extra irrigation to leach** salt below the roots, plus drainage to carry it away.
- Salt sources: the soil itself, saline irrigation water, rising groundwater, seawater intrusion near the coast.
**Benefits of drainage:** better **aeration**; a **deeper root zone**; **warmer** soil, so faster nutrient release; more **micro-organism** activity.

cards.title: 3.5.6 Types of drainage
body: - **Surface drainage**: shallow **open ditches** leading into bigger collector drains; fields are **graded** to slope towards them.
- **Sub-surface drainage**: buried **perforated pipes** (laterals → collectors → mains → sump); used where natural drainage is poor, to **leach salts** and to **lower a shallow water table**.
- **Vertical drainage**: **pumping** groundwater out of dug or tube wells; works where poorly permeable topsoil lies over deep permeable subsoil.
- **Bio-drainage**: planting thirsty trees (e.g. **eucalyptus**) and crops that pump water out through transpiration.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which type of drainage system uses trees with high water requirements, such as Eucalyptus species, to naturally transpire excess water?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Bio-drainage is a biological drainage method where deep-rooted vegetation with high transpiration rates (such as *Eucalyptus* species) is planted to draw up and remove excess water from waterlogged soils.

**Conclusion**
This biological system is **Bio-drainage**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Why is proper soil drainage essential for fruit tree production?

options.A: It prevents the leaves from absorbing too much nitrogen.
options.B: Fruit tree roots suffocate and can die if waterlogged for even a week.
options.C: It increases the atmospheric wind speed around the orchard.
options.D: It prevents the soil from compacting under the weight of the fruit.
options.E: It eliminates the need for any subsequent organic manuring.

cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Fruit trees are highly sensitive to waterlogging. Even on excellent soils, just one week of waterlogging is enough to suffocate and kill fruit tree roots, causing a severe loss of productivity.

**Conclusion**
Therefore, drainage is essential because **roots suffocate and die if waterlogged for even a week**.

tips.text: Soil and water conservation refers to practices involving all the human activities aimed at reducing the loss of soil from the land, as well as protecting and maintaining the water supply.
It concerns practical farming measures taken in order to protect land from damage and prevent water wastage.
The speed and extent of soil degradation depends on different factors, such as types of soils, relief, climate and the intensity of land use.
Loss of land-resource productivity is an important problem in Eritrea and, coupled with a growing population, is likely to become critical in the future.
Diverse areas are affected differently by soil degradation.
The Highlands of Eritrea are the areas of greatest livestock density and where major land degradation occurs.

Continued deterioration of land leads to a permanent decrease in its biological potential and deterioration of living conditions for the inhabitants.
Land degradation is both a process and a phenomenon.

Mechanical: Contour ploughing, terraces and bunds, check dams, cut-off drains, sub-surface dams in sandy wadis.

questions.q: While inspecting a gently sloping cropland near Keren, a farmer finds many small, shallow, parallel channels running down the field, each only about 20 cm deep. Which type of water erosion is this, and why can the farmer still correct it with ordinary tillage?

options.A: Splash erosion, because raindrop impact has formed a hard surface crust
options.B: Sheet erosion, because the channels are broad, thin sheets of flowing water
options.C: Rill erosion, because these are small, shallow, concentrated flow channels that ordinary farm tillage can smooth out
options.D: Gully erosion, because the channels are narrow and deep and cannot be destroyed by normal tillage

why: **Recall the classification of water erosion.** The unit divides water erosion into four types: splash (raindrop) erosion, sheet erosion, rill erosion and gully erosion.

**Match the field evidence to a type.** The field shows small, shallow, concentrated flow paths (channels) rather than craters from raindrop impact or a uniform thin sheet of moving water. Small, shallow, concentrated flow paths are the defining feature of rill erosion.

**Check the depth against the unit data.** The unit records rill channels as up to $$30\text{ cm}$$ deep, so the measured 20 cm depth falls inside the rill range, while gullies are $$1 - 150\text{ meters}$$ deep.
**Decide on correctability.** The unit states that rills are temporary and can easily be smoothed out by ordinary farm tillage operations, unlike gullies, which cannot be destroyed by normal tillage.

**Evaluate the distractors.** A is wrong because splash erosion creates small craters and a hard crust, not channels. B is wrong because sheet erosion removes soil uniformly in broad, thin sheets, not in defined small channels. D is wrong because the channels are shallow and the unit reserves the non-tillable, deep category for gullies.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: On a bare, sloping plot at Tsorona, raindrops strike the unprotected soil and small crater-like marks appear, with loose soil particles splashed onto the leaves of young maize. The soil surface later dries into a hard crust. Which type of water erosion is responsible?
why: **Recall the four types of water erosion.** Water erosion occurs as splash, sheet, rill and gully erosion, distinguished by how the soil is detached and moved.
**Identify the detachment mechanism.** Here the soil is detached by the direct impact of raindrops on bare soil, which is the definition of splash (raindrop) erosion.

**Confirm with the unit description.** The unit describes splash erosion as producing small craters on bare soil, splashing soil onto plant leaves, destroying soil structure and forming a hard crust on dry soil - all features observed on the plot.
**Rule out the other types.** There is no uniform removal of soil down the slope in thin sheets (sheet), no concentrated channels (rill) and no deep, incised channel (gully).

questions.q: A forester uses a line level to check the slope of a gently sloping cropland near Keren before laying out contour bunds. The two identical sticks are set $$10\text{ meters}$$ apart, and the reading on the stick at the lower ground position is $$0.9\text{ meters}$$ greater than the reading on the stick at the higher ground position. Calculate the percentage slope of the plot and state, with justification, whether the site is suitable for contour bunds.
questions.answer: Percentage slope = $$9\%$$; this is slightly steeper than the $$2\% - 8\%$$ ideal range for contour bunds, so bund spacing must be tightened or a stronger physical measure such as hillside terracing used.
why: **Identify what the line level measures.** The unit describes the line level as two identical $$1.5\text{-meter}$$ sticks connected by a $$10\text{-meter}$$ cotton string with a small spirit level suspended in the middle. Because the string is exactly $$10\text{ meters}$$ long, the horizontal interval (HI) is the fixed stick spacing of $$10\text{ meters}$$.

**Obtain the vertical interval.** The vertical interval (VI) is the difference in elevation between the two points. Since both sticks stand vertically, the difference in reading on the sticks equals the difference in ground elevation: $$\text{VI} = 0.9\text{ meters}$$.
**Name the percentage slope formula.** The unit gives $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{\text{VI}}{\text{HI}}\right) \times 100$$.
**Substitute the measured values.** $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{0.9}{10}\right) \times 100 = 0.09 \times 100 = 9\%$$.

**Compare the slope with the ideal site for contour bunds.** The unit table states that contour bunds intercept surface runoff and encourage infiltration on gently sloping croplands of $$2\% - 8\%$$ slope. The computed slope of $$9\%$$ is slightly steeper than that ideal range.

**Conclude with a justified recommendation.** The plot is at $$9\%$$ slope, just above the $$2\% - 8\%$$ band for which contour bunds are the recommended physical measure. Contour bunds would need closer spacing and careful design, and on such a slope a stronger structural measure such as hillside terraces, which break slope length and trap water and sediment on sloping cultivated hills, should be considered.

questions.q: While surveying a field at Mendefera with a line level whose two sticks are $$10\text{ meters}$$ apart, the assistant records the difference in stick readings as $$0.4\text{ meters}$$. Compute the percentage slope of the field and decide whether it falls within the slope range for which the unit recommends contour bunds.
questions.answer: Percentage slope = $$4\%$$; this lies within the $$2\% - 8\%$$ range, so contour bunds are suitable
why: **Fix the horizontal interval.** The line level uses a $$10\text{-meter}$$ string, so the sticks are $$10\text{ meters}$$ apart and $$\text{HI} = 10\text{ meters}$$.
**Read off the vertical interval.** The difference in stick readings equals the difference in ground elevation, so $$\text{VI} = 0.4\text{ meters}$$.
**State the formula.** $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{\text{VI}}{\text{HI}}\right) \times 100$$.
**Substitute and compute.** $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{0.4}{10}\right) \times 100 = 0.04 \times 100 = 4\%$$.
**Judge suitability.** $$4\%$$ falls inside the $$2\% - 8\%$$ gently sloping cropland range given for contour bunds, so the site is suitable for this physical measure.

questions.q: On a hillside above Asmara, two points on the ground lie $$50\text{ meters}$$ apart horizontally, and a telescopic level shows that the upper point is $$7.5\text{ meters}$$ higher than the lower point. Compute the percentage slope of this hillside and explain what such a slope means for the choice between contour bunds and hillside terraces.
questions.answer: Percentage slope = $$15\%$$; this far exceeds the $$2\% - 8\%$$ range for contour bunds, so hillside terraces (which break slope length and trap water and sediment) are the appropriate physical measure
why: **Identify the given intervals.** The horizontal distance between the two points is $$\text{HI} = 50\text{ meters}$$ and the elevation difference is $$\text{VI} = 7.5\text{ meters}$$.
**Apply the percentage slope formula.** $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{\text{VI}}{\text{HI}}\right) \times 100$$.
**Substitute and compute.** $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{7.5}{50}\right) \times 100 = 0.15 \times 100 = 15\%$$.

**Interpret the result on the landscape.** A $$15\%$$ slope is nearly twice the upper limit of the $$2\% - 8\%$$ band listed for contour bunds, so bunds alone would not safely handle the runoff on this hillside.

**Select the matching measure.** The unit lists hillside terraces as the physical measure for sloping, cultivated or uncultivated hills because they break slope length, trap water and sediment, and create flat planting steps - the correct choice for a $$15\%$$ hillside.

questions.q: Describe the transition of water erosion from splash erosion to the formation of a highly advanced gully system on a bare, sloping farm plot in the highlands. In your answer, name each stage in order, state the characteristic feature and approximate depth or scale of each, and explain how the farmer could detect the earliest stage of uniform soil removal before channels appear.
questions.answer: The sequence is splash (raindrop) erosion (micro-scale craters, hard crust, particles splashed up to $$1.5\text{ m}$$) then sheet erosion (uniform removal in broad, thin sheets, detectable early by soil pedestals) then rill erosion (small, shallow concentrated channels up to $$30\text{ cm}$$ deep, removable by ordinary tillage) then gully erosion (narrow, deep channels of $$1 - 150\text{ m}$$ that fragment the land and cannot be destroyed by normal tillage).
why: **Start with detachment by raindrop impact.** The process begins with splash (raindrop) erosion, the detachment and airborne movement of small soil particles caused by direct raindrop impact on bare soil. On a micro-scale it produces small craters, destroys soil structure and forms a hard crust on dry soil; the unit notes raindrops can strike bare soil at speeds up to $$30\text{ kilometers per hour}$$ and splash particles up to $$1.5\text{ meters}$$ horizontally.

**Move to uniform removal as sheet erosion.** Once detached, particles are removed uniformly down the slope by water flowing overland in broad, thin sheets rather than in defined channels. Sheet erosion strips very thin layers, removing the most fertile topsoil and organic matter and exposing stone bases.

**Explain how to detect the sheet stage early.** The unit pro-tip advises looking for soil pedestals - tiny columns of soil capped by small stones or wood chips that have protected the soil directly underneath from raindrop impact. Their appearance signals that the surrounding soil is being stripped away in thin sheets before any channels form.

**Describe the appearance of concentrated flow paths.** As overland flow concentrates, rill erosion develops small, shallow, concentrated flow paths that appear as many small, parallel channels across the field, up to $$30\text{ cm}$$ deep. Rills are temporary and can be easily smoothed out by ordinary tillage, so the unit pro-tip warns that if left untreated for even one rainy season they merge and deepen.

**Explain the final, advanced stage.** In the advanced stage the runoff flows in narrow, deep channels during or immediately after heavy rains, producing gullies. Gullies range from $$1\text{ to }2\text{ meters}$$ to over $$75\text{ meters}$$ deep (the unit table gives $$1 - 150\text{ meters}$$), with wide, steep, unstable walls that cannot be destroyed by normal tillage operations.

**State the consequence and the conclusion.** The gully divides the land into fragments and stops machinery movement, making reclamation extremely difficult and expensive. The correct conclusion is that the stages form a continuous, accelerating chain - splash to sheet to rill to gully - so intervention at the rill stage (or earlier, by spotting soil pedestals and applying biological or physical conservation measures) is far cheaper than reclaiming a mature gully.

questions.q: Explain how wind erosion acts on a dry, bare lowland plain such as the eastern dry lowlands, naming its two main effects and describing the damage each does to soil and crops.
questions.answer: Wind erosion acts through deflation, the lifting and removal of loose, light soil particles to another region, and abrasion, the wearing away of plants, rocks and structures by suspended soil particles carried in high-velocity winds; together they strip topsoil and damage seedlings.
why: **State where wind erosion occurs.** The unit states that wind erosion occurs primarily in arid and semi-arid climates where the soil is dry and unprotected by vegetation, which describes the dry lowlands receiving only about $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$ of soil loss by wind.
**Define the first effect.** Deflation is the lifting and removal of loose, light soil particles to another region. It is the primary cause of topsoil blowing away from dry lowland fields.

**Define the second effect.** Abrasion is the wearing away of plants, rocks and structures by suspended soil particles carried in high-velocity winds, and the unit table records it as sand abrasion on seedlings.

**Conclude on the agricultural impact.** Because the dry lowlands have only wind - not rainfall runoff - as the primary causative agent, the conservation response must protect the surface, for example by maintaining vegetative cover and mulch rather than by constructing water-intercepting structures.

questions.q: Explain how rainfall and topography combine to make the Eritrean highlands the most erosion-prone area in the unit's comparison of regions, and state the specific consequences this has for crop production there.
questions.answer: In the highlands, high and intense rainfall produces large volumes of runoff that steep topography accelerates downslope, giving an estimated soil loss of $$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$, the highest of the four regions; the consequences are exposed plant roots, severe yield reduction and loss of topsoil.
why: **Recall the two controlling factors.** The unit states that the speed and extent of soil degradation depend on factors such as soil types, topography, climate and the intensity of land use - here climate (rainfall) and topography (slope) are decisive.

**Explain the role of the rainfall factor.** Rainfall in these highland areas supplies the water that detaches particles by raindrop impact and then carries them downslope as runoff, so water is listed as the primary causative agent for the highlands.

**Explain the role of the topographic factor.** Slope steepness increases the velocity of runoff, so the water has more energy to detach and transport soil. The unit records measured soil loss on steep slopes of $$3.4\text{ to }84.5\text{ tons per hectare per year}$$, with a mean of $$42\text{ tons per hectare per year}$$ - about $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil annually and roughly $$20\text{ times}$$ the soil replacement rate.

**Apply the regional comparison.** In the unit's table the highlands have the highest estimated loss at $$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$, well above the moist lowlands ($$47$$), the eastern escarpment ($$37$$) and the dry lowlands ($$6$$), confirming the highlands as the most erosion-prone region.

**State the agricultural consequences.** The table lists exposed plant roots, severe yield reduction and loss of topsoil for the highlands. The unit adds that erosion depletes nitrogen and phosphorus, lowers water retention capacity, reduces soil depth and exposes roots, making crops highly vulnerable to drought.

questions.q:
A soil conservation team compares two Eritrean sites using the unit's regional soil-loss figures. Site A is highland farmland whose measured loss falls at the lower end of the highland range given in the unit ($$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$). Site B is dry lowland farmland losing $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$.
(a) Calculate how many times greater the soil loss at Site A is than at Site B.
(b) The unit also notes that under natural conditions $$1\text{ centimeter}$$ of fertile topsoil takes $$100\text{ to }400\text{ years}$$ to form, and that a loss of about $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil per year represents approximately $$20\text{ times}$$ the possible soil replacement rate. Using the mid-point of the formation range ($$250\text{ years}$$ per centimeter), calculate the average annual topsoil formation in millimetres per year, and hence explain in one sentence how Site A's loss compares with it.
questions.answer: (a) Site A ($$50\text{ tons/ha/year}$$) loses about $$8.3\text{ times}$$ as much soil as Site B ($$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$). (b) Using the mid-point of $$250\text{ years}$$ per centimeter, natural topsoil formation averages $$0.04\text{ mm per year}$$, so Site A's loss of roughly $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil per year is about $$100\text{ times}$$ faster than the soil can be replaced.
why: **Extract the soil-loss figures for the two sites.** The unit table gives the highlands an estimated soil loss of $$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$ and the dry lowlands $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$. Site A lies at the lower end of the highland range, so its loss is $$50\text{ tons/ha/year}$$; Site B loses $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$.
**State the ratio to be computed.** The required comparison is a ratio: $$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{\text{Loss at Site A}}{\text{Loss at Site B}}$$.
**Substitute and carry out the division.** $$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{50}{6} = 8.33$$, i.e. approximately $$8.3\text{ times}$$.

**Convert the natural formation range into an annual rate.** Under natural conditions $$1\text{ centimeter}$$ ($$= 10\text{ mm}$$) of topsoil needs $$100\text{ to }400\text{ years}$$. Taking the mid-point of $$250\text{ years}$$ per centimeter, the average annual formation is $$\dfrac{10\text{ mm}}{250\text{ years}} = 0.04\text{ mm per year}$$.

**Relate the computed loss rate to the formation rate.** The unit states that a loss of approximately $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil per year is about $$20\text{ times}$$ the possible soil replacement rate. This is consistent with the computed formation rate: $$\dfrac{4\text{ mm}}{0.04\text{ mm per year}} = 100$$ - that is, at the lower-end highland loss of $$50\text{ t/ha/year}$$ the soil is still being removed many times faster than the $$0.04\text{ mm per year}$$ at which fertile topsoil forms naturally.

**State the agronomic consequence.** Because accumulation cannot keep pace with removal, the topsoil layer thins progressively. This matches the unit's description of land degradation as a continuous process marked by progressive weakening of the physical, chemical and biological potential of land, and of erosion causing nutrient depletion (especially nitrogen and phosphorus), lower water retention, reduced soil depth and exposed plant roots.

**Draw the conservation conclusion.** The comparison shows that Site A loses roughly $$8.3\text{ times}$$ as much soil as Site B, and still loses topsoil dozens of times faster than nature rebuilds it, so a physical or biological soil and water conservation measure - for example hillside terraces on the sloping highland plot - is required rather than relying on natural soil formation.

questions.q:
Two farms are compared using the unit's regional figures. Farm X lies in the highlands, where the measured soil loss is at the upper end of the unit's highland range ($$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$). Farm Y lies in the dry lowlands, where the primary causative agent is wind and the estimated loss is $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$.
(a) Calculate the ratio of Farm X's soil loss to Farm Y's.
(b) Using the unit figure of about $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil lost per year at the mean steep-slope loss rate, and a natural formation time of $$100\text{ years}$$ for $$1\text{ centimeter}$$ of topsoil, calculate the annual natural formation rate and state how many times larger the loss rate is.
questions.answer: (a) $$\dfrac{100}{6} = 16.7$$, so about $$16.7\text{ times}$$ (roughly $$17\text{ times}$$). (b) $$\dfrac{10\text{ mm}}{100\text{ years}} = 0.1\text{ mm per year}$$, so the $$4\text{ mm per year}$$ loss is $$40\text{ times}$$ the natural formation rate
why: **Read the required values from the unit.** The upper end of the highland range is $$100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$, so Farm X loses $$100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$; the dry lowland figure is $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$, so Farm Y loses $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$.
**Compute the ratio.** $$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{100}{6} = 16.7$$, so Farm X loses about $$16.7\text{ times}$$ as much soil as Farm Y.
**Convert formation time to an annual rate.** $$1\text{ centimeter} = 10\text{ mm}$$ forms in $$100\text{ years}$$, so the natural formation rate is $$\dfrac{10}{100} = 0.1\text{ mm per year}$$.

**Compare loss with formation.** $$\dfrac{4\text{ mm per year}}{0.1\text{ mm per year}} = 40$$, so the loss rate is $$40\text{ times}$$ the natural formation rate at the fastest possible natural formation.

**Interpret the result.** Even under the most favourable natural soil-building conditions in the unit ($$100\text{ years}$$ per centimeter), erosion on steep highland farmland removes topsoil far faster than it forms, which is why the unit calls topsoil a precious, slow-forming resource and why conservation measures are indispensable.

questions.q:
A highland catchment of $$200\text{ hectares}$$ is losing topsoil by water erosion at the unit's mean rate for steep slopes of $$42\text{ tons per hectare per year}$$.
(a) Calculate the total annual soil loss from the catchment in tons.
(b) Given that this mean rate corresponds to an annual loss of approximately $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil, calculate the total volume of topsoil lost each year in cubic metres (take $$1\text{ m}^3$$ of topsoil $$= 1.3\text{ tons}$$), and express your answer to the nearest whole cubic metre.
(c) State one conservation measure from the unit that would directly reduce this loss on the sloping cultivated land, and one that would trap the sediment already being carried away.
questions.answer: (a) $$200 \times 42 = 8\,400\text{ tons per year}$$. (b) $$\dfrac{8\,400}{1.3} = 6\,461.5$$, so approximately $$6\,462\text{ m}^3$$ of topsoil per year. (c) Hillside terraces (or contour bunds) on the sloping cultivated land reduce detachment and runoff, while check dams built across active gullies trap the sediment and slow the water.
why: **Identify the mean loss rate and area.** The unit reports a mean soil loss of $$42\text{ tons per hectare per year}$$ on steep slopes, and the catchment area is $$200\text{ hectares}$$.
**Compute the total annual soil loss.** $$\text{Total loss} = 42\text{ tons/ha/year} \times 200\text{ ha} = 8\,400\text{ tons per year}$$.

**Convert tons of soil to volume.** Using $$1\text{ m}^3 = 1.3\text{ tons}$$, the volume is $$\dfrac{8\,400\text{ tons}}{1.3\text{ tons/m}^3} = 6\,461.5\text{ m}^3$$, which rounds to approximately $$6\,462\text{ m}^3$$ per year.

**Link the loss to the thinning topsoil layer.** The unit notes that the mean steep-slope loss represents an annual loss of about $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil, roughly $$20\text{ times}$$ the possible soil replacement rate, so this volume represents a layer of fertile topsoil that natural formation cannot replace within a human lifetime.

**Select measures that reduce and trap the loss.** Hillside terraces are a physical measure that breaks slope length and traps water and sediment on sloping cultivated hills, and contour bunds intercept surface runoff and encourage infiltration on gently sloping croplands. Check dams are built across gullies to slow water velocity and trap sediment, preventing the gullies from widening.

body: Agriculture can be defined as an industry involving the organization of resources such as land, capital, labour and management for the production of food and non-food agricultural products.

cards.title: 4.1.2 The Importance of Farm Management
body: The term “farm management” comprises two words: “farm” and “management”.
A “farm” includes all the land on which a person performs some kind of agricultural operation, either by his/her own labour or family labour or hired employees.

“Management”, on the other hand, is the function of combining ideas, physical and human resources, and processing these efficiently to achieve stated objectives such as an increase in the productivity of farm output, or the profitability of the farm.
In commercial farms, the main objective is the maximization of profit of the farm or the minimization of the cost of production.

cards.title: 4.1.3 Agriculture as Industry
body: People work in different activities such as in teaching, providing health services, production of crops, shoes, clothing and in raising livestock, etc.
With economic development, agriculture has taken on a broader meaning.
Additionally, a good knowledge of the interrelationship between agriculture, the environment and sustainable development is crucial.
**Agriculture** is the most important industry in developing countries.

cards.title: 4.1.4 Factors of Production
body: **Economics** is the study of how people allocate their limited resources in order to satisfy their unlimited wants over time.
Land: This is the most important factor of production for a farmer.
A farmer must have land to grow food or raise livestock.
Labour: This is the productive contribution of humans who work, both mentally and physically, on the farm.

cards.title: 4.1.5 Basic Economic Principles
body: The relationship between inputs and outputs can be described as a production function.

The production function is thus a technical and mathematical relationship describing the manner and extent to which a particular product depends upon the quantities of input(s) or services of inputs used under a given state of technology.
Production functions can be expressed in three forms: tabular, graphic and algebraic.
Where y represents a dependent variable, such as crop yield, and x represents an independent variable, such as fertiliser, with ƒ denoting “function of”.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The law of diminishing returns states that, as more units of a variable input (e.g. fertilizer) are added to a fixed input (land):

options.C: each extra unit eventually adds less and less to total output
options.D: output always increases by the same amount

cards.why:
**Step 1:** At first extra fertilizer may raise yield strongly.

**Step 2:** After a point, each additional bag gives a smaller increase in yield (marginal product falls).

**Step 3:** Answer: each extra unit eventually adds less and less.

**Tip:** A farmer should stop adding input when the value of the extra output equals the cost of the extra input.

cards.title: 4.2.1 Farm Accounting Records
body: **An inventory** is a statement in which all the physical assets of the farm business and their monetary values are recorded.
The inventory should be prepared at least once a year.
When physically measuring assets, numbers and quantities should be established i.e. how many hectares of land, livestock, bags of grain, machinery and equipment, etc.
In order to calculate the monetary values of assets, all the physical assets should be valued and depreciation deducted.

cards.title: 4.2.2 Physical Production, Labour and Machinery Records
body: Production records are valuable to diagnose problems and identify opportunities for business.
The statements most commonly used are crop cultivation, livestock, labour and machinery statements.
Crop cultivation statements contain information on a specific crop or type of fruit that is being cultivated.
The various field or orchard numbers, areas, yield potential and soil analysis of the land used for cultivating that particular crop or fruit are recorded.

cards.title: 4.2.3 Financial Statements
body: A full set of financial statements would consist of a balance sheet, an income statement and a cash-flow statement.
**A balance sheet** is a financial statement which reflects the financial position of a farm business on a specific date (at a specific moment in time).
The relations of assets, liabilities and capital represent the financial position of farm enterprises.
**The balance sheet** is the systematic presentation of these three aspects for a specific date, with each individual item being identified and linked to a monetary value.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In a classical agricultural production function, which stage of production represents the 'rational zone' where the profit-maximizing input level is located?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Stage I is a zone of under-utilization where input efficiency is still rising. Stage III is a zone of waste where adding more inputs decreases total product (negative MP). Stage II is the only rational zone of production because the marginal product is positive but decreasing, and the optimal profit-maximizing point (where MVP = Px) lies within its boundaries.

**Conclusion**
Thus, the rational zone is **Stage II**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Under what conditions is a farm said to be insolvent or bankrupt on its balance sheet?

options.A: When total revenues are lower than variable costs.
options.B: When net worth or owner's equity is negative.
options.C: When current assets exceed long-term liabilities.
options.D: When there is a net loss on the income statement.
options.E: When no physical inventory is kept.

cards.why:
**Reasoning**
A balance sheet reflects the accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Net worth (owner's equity) is calculated as Assets minus Liabilities. If a farm's total liabilities (debts) exceed its total assets, the net worth becomes negative, which means the farm is insolvent or bankrupt.

**Conclusion**
Therefore, insolvency occurs **When net worth or owner's equity is negative**.

cards.q: Which of the following are considered non-cash costs and are therefore excluded from a cash-flow statement?

**Reasoning**
A cash-flow statement records only actual cash inflows and cash outflows at the time they occur. Depreciation is an accounting entry representing the loss of value of an asset over time and does not involve any actual cash transaction. Therefore, it is excluded from cash-flow statements.

**Conclusion**
Thus, the excluded non-cash cost is **Machinery depreciation**.

cards.title: 4.3.1 Planning
body: Farm planning is fundamental to the management process, because farming has become a complex business.

Land: Major factors to be considered for land include type of land ownership (communal, government or private land), fertility of land, size of cultivable and non-cultivable land, and location of land to the major markets.
Labour: : Labour needed for particular farm operations must be assessed for the farming season (specific months or year).
As labour is heterogeneous, the total labour required is estimated based on person-days.

cards.title: 4.3.2 Decision-making
body: The main objective of farm planning and budgeting is to make better decisions.
Decisions, which are based on a prepared plan, are better than decisions that are made without any plan.

cards.title: 4.3.3 Implementation
body: Once a budget is prepared and decision made, then the plan must be implemented.

cards.title: 4.3.4 Monitoring
body: When a farmer decides to implement his or her planned farm activities, he or she should monitor the farm activities so that they will have adequate farm records that enable them to periodically evaluate the farm outcome relative to the plan.

cards.title: 4.3.5 Evaluation and Appraisal
body: Once the farm plan of action is implemented, it has to be evaluated at the end of the crop cyclic to establish to what extent the farm plan has been achieved by comparing the plan’s profitability against the actual profit of the farm.

cards.title: 4.4.1 The Importance of Community-based Organizations
body: In many societies, farmers pool their resources and work together on their farms during sowing, weeding, harvesting and threshing.
Community-based organizations (CBOs) are membership organizations made up of individuals who have joined to meet their common interests.
Examples include women’s groups, credit associations, youth clubs, farmer co-operatives and so on.

cards.title: 4.4.2 Types of CBO
body: **An association** is a self-help organization (SHO) which aims at satisfying the collective objective of its members only.

**A co-operative** is an autonomous association of persons (consumers or producers) united voluntarily to meet their common economic, social and cultural objectives through jointly owned and democratically controlled enterprises.
Co-operation is based on close personal ties and mutual trust.
Generally, co-operatives have an economic purpose, are owned and controlled by the members, are run for the benefit of members, and are not charities or state-directed organizations.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The democratic principle that distinguishes cooperatives from private joint-stock business corporations is:

options.A: Voting power based on the number of capital shares owned.
options.C: Top managers make all business decisions without member input.
options.D: Only government officers are allowed to vote.
options.E: No voting is allowed in cooperatives.

cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Unlike private corporations where voting power is proportional to the number of financial shares owned, cooperatives follow the democratic principle of equality: "one member, one vote," regardless of how much capital a member has contributed.

**Conclusion**
Thus, the core democratic principle is **One member, one vote**.

glossary.meaning: Agriculture is the most important industry in developing countries.
Capital is a very important factor of production because it is a vehicle for development.

tips.text: Agriculture can be defined as an industry involving the organization of resources such as land, capital, labour and management for the production of food and raw materials.

Farm management can be defined as a science which deals with the proper use of scarce farm resources, having alternative uses to obtain the maximum profit and family satisfaction on a continuous basis from the farm.
The functions of a farm manager can be summarized generally as those of planning, implementation and control.
In commercial farms, the most desirable objective is maximization of profit or the minimization production costs.
In subsistence farms, profit is not the main objective.
Production is mainly for achieving self-sufficiency or earning a certain level of income.

The most common problems in the field of farm management and planning in Eritrea are the small size of farm businesses, traditional methods of farming, inadequate capital, slow adoption of innovations, inadequate input supplies and use, low managerial skills, and poor communication and markets.
Resources are inputs used in the production of the goods and services that are used by farmers to produce agricultural commodities.
The characteristics of resources are economic value, limited supply and alternative uses.
The most important production factors include land, labour, capital and management.

questions.q: A vegetable farm near Asmara owns a tractor, an irrigation system and a farm store building. Which one of the following items would be classified as working capital and NOT as fixed capital on this farm?

options.A: Fertilizer purchased for the coming tomato season
options.C: Irrigation system fitted with a diesel pump
options.D: Farm store building for harvested vegetables

why: **Recall the definition of capital.** Capital is the human-made factor of production. The unit divides it into fixed capital (assets used over many years) and working capital (cash or inputs used up in a single production cycle).

**Apply the test of a single production cycle.** Fixed capital such as tractors, buildings and irrigation systems gives service over many years and depreciates over time. Working capital such as seeds, fertilizers and pesticides is consumed within one season.

**Screen each option.** B (tractor) and C (irrigation system) are listed in the unit as fixed capital, and D (farm store building) is also a building used over many years. None of them is used up in one season.
**Select and conclude.** Only A, fertilizer for the coming tomato season, is an input used up inside a single production cycle, so it is working capital and not fixed capital.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: On a dairy farm in the Eritrean highlands, which one of the following is working capital rather than fixed capital?
questions.answer: A. Animal feed bought for the current milking cycle
why: **State the classification rule.** Working capital is cash or inputs that are used up in a single production cycle; fixed capital is used over many years.
**Check each item.** The milking shed and the milking machine are used over many years, so both are fixed capital.
**Test the remaining option.** Animal feed is consumed by the cows within the current cycle and must be replaced continuously, so it is used up in one cycle.
**Conclude.** Animal feed for the current cycle is working capital, therefore the answer is A.

questions.q: A crop farm keeps the following on its records: family labour, a harrow, maize seed and a pickup truck. Which of these belongs to the working capital category?
why: **Separate the factors of production.** Family labour is the labour factor, while the harrow, the pickup truck and the maize seed are all capital (human-made assets).
**Apply the single-cycle test.** The harrow and the pickup truck are used over many years, so they are fixed capital, not working capital.
**Identify the single-cycle input.** Maize seed is planted and used up within one production cycle, exactly like the seeds and fertilizers named in the unit.
**Conclude.** Maize seed is working capital, so the answer is C.

questions.q: A farmer at Keren is considering replacing the local wheat variety on one hectare with a new high-yielding variety. The change would raise seed cost by $$30\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and fertilizer cost by $$9\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$, and it would reduce the cost of hired labour for weeding by $$2\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$. Yield would rise by $$12\text{ quintals}$$, each selling at $$1\,200\text{ Nakfa}$$, but the crop would no longer be sold as local seed, which used to bring an extra $$3\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. Using a partial budget, decide whether the farmer should adopt the new variety, and state the net change in returns.
questions.answer: The farmer should NOT adopt the new variety, because Added Returns + Reduced Costs ($$16\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$) are less than Added Costs + Reduced Returns ($$42\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$); the change would make returns worse by $$25\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$.
why: **Name the tool and its decision rule.** This is a minor single-enterprise change on one hectare, so a partial budget is the correct tool. The rule from the unit is: implement if $$\text{Added Returns} + \text{Reduced Costs} > \text{Added Costs} + \text{Reduced Returns}$$.
**Compute total added returns.** The extra yield is $$12\text{ quintals} \times 1\,200\text{ Nakfa} = 14\,400\text{ Nakfa}$$, so Added Returns $$= 14\,400\text{ Nakfa}$$.
**Compute total reduced costs.** Hired weeding labour falls by $$2\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$, so Reduced Costs $$= 2\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$. The left-hand side is $$14\,400 + 2\,500 = 16\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$.

**Compute the added costs and reduced returns.** Added Costs are extra seed plus extra fertilizer: $$30\,000 + 9\,800 = 39\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$. Reduced Returns are the lost local-seed premium of $$3\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. The right-hand side is $$39\,800 + 3\,000 = 42\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$.

**Compare and conclude.** $$16\,900\text{ Nakfa} < 42\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$, so the right-hand side is larger. The change fails the partial-budget test by $$42\,800 - 16\,900 = 25\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$, and the farmer should not adopt the new variety.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A farmer at Massawa plans to buy a small diesel pump to irrigate one hectare of vegetables. The pump costs $$18\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and annual fuel and maintenance add $$4\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$, while it would save $$7\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ a year in hired watering labour. Extra vegetables worth $$21\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ a year would be produced. Use a partial budget to decide whether the pump should be bought, and give the net change per year.
questions.answer: Buy the pump: Added Returns + Reduced Costs = $$21\,000 + 7\,000 = 28\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ exceeds Added Costs = $$22\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$, giving a net gain of $$5\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$ per year.
why: **Identify the tool and rule.** Buying one new tool for one hectare is a minor change, so use a partial budget: implement if $$\text{Added Returns} + \text{Reduced Costs} > \text{Added Costs} + \text{Reduced Returns}$$.
**Add up the benefit side.** Added Returns are the extra vegetables, $$21\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$; Reduced Costs are the saved watering labour, $$7\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. Total $$= 28\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.
**Add up the cost side.** Added Costs are the pump price plus fuel and maintenance: $$18\,000 + 4\,500 = 22\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$. There are no reduced returns in this case.

questions.q: On 31 December a farm business near Asmara reports current assets of $$25\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and long-term assets of $$75\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. Its current liabilities are $$8\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and its long-term bank loan is $$12\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. (a) Calculate the farm's net worth (capital). (b) State whether the farm is solvent, and explain what the balance sheet would have to show for the farm to be insolvent.
questions.answer: (a) Net worth = $$100\,000 - 20\,000 = 80\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. (b) The farm is solvent because net worth is positive; it would be insolvent only if total liabilities exceeded total assets, giving a negative net worth.
why: **State the balance-sheet equation.** A balance sheet reflects the financial position on a specific date and follows the accounting equation $$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Capital (Net Worth)}$$.
**Total the assets.** Current assets plus long-term assets: $$25\,000 + 75\,000 = 100\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.
**Total the liabilities.** Current liabilities plus long-term liabilities: $$8\,000 + 12\,000 = 20\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.
**Solve for net worth.** Rearranging the equation gives Net Worth $$= \text{Assets} - \text{Liabilities} = 100\,000 - 20\,000 = 80\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.

**Interpret solvency.** Net worth is positive ($$80\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$), so assets exceed liabilities and the farm is solvent. It would be insolvent (bankrupt) only if liabilities exceeded assets, that is, if net worth were negative.
